title: None of it is yours
hook: wealth, spouse, property: you call them yours, but none goes with you (Salok M9, ang 1426)

segments.voice: Yesterday, auadh, and your line: the days slip. Did you look at a clock and really see it? If the days are slipping, what are we holding as they go? Today's salok asks about the word mine. Day five hundred ninety-one.

Clearing out a parent's house after they've died is a strange job. Every drawer is full of things that mattered to someone. The good china saved for guests who rarely came. A box of receipts from 1987. A coat that still smells like them. Each object was mine to someone for decades. Now it's a question: keep, give, throw away. And the one who called it all mine isn't here to decide. Guru Tegh Bahadur's fifth salok stands in exactly that room, and says out loud what that room already shows.
screen: `CLEARING OUT A PARENT'S HOUSE.` → `EVERY DRAWER WAS SOMEONE'S MINE.` → `THE FIFTH SALOK.`

segments.voice: The salok begins dhan daaraa sampat sagal, jin apunee kar maan. In paraphrase: wealth, spouse, all your property, all the things you take to be your own: not one of them is your companion. Says Nanak, know this as true. Dhan is wealth. Sampat is property, possessions. Daaraa is wife, or spouse. And the key phrase is apunee kar maan: to treat as one's own. That's what the salok is really looking at. Not the things, but the word mine stamped on them. Now, the salok lists a spouse beside the money, and that can sound harsh. But the Sikh path is lived in families; the ninth Guru himself was a husband and father. The salok isn't saying don't love your husband or wife. It's saying that even the person closest to you isn't a possession, and doesn't travel with you through death. Hearing it that way, it's almost tender. The people we love were never ours to own. They were gifts, given for a while. And notice the word companion, sangee. The salok isn't asking you to throw anything away. It's asking: who walks with you all the way? On day five hundred twelve, Sukhmani said the earned Name and the self your deeds shaped are what go along. Guru Tegh Bahadur's couplet makes the same point from the other side, by naming what stays behind. The practical result is a lighter grip. You can enjoy a good house, love a family, earn honestly, and still say, quietly: this is lent to me. None of it goes. Then the ring goes back on, the house stays a home, and the word mine gets a little quieter.
screen: `DHAN, DAARAA, SAMPAT.` · `APUNEE KAR MAAN: CALLING IT MINE.` · `PEOPLE AREN'T POSSESSIONS.` · `WHAT IS LENT, NOT OWNED.` · then, large: `NONE OF IT GOES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold one possession lightly. Pick up something you own and care about: a ring, a watch, a mug, your phone. Hold it in an open hand. Feel its weight. Think about where it came from and who made it. Then say quietly to yourself: this is lent to me. Notice what happens in your chest. Does the grip tighten, or loosen? Put it down gently and sit with empty hands for the rest of the time. If you pray, you can give thanks to Waheguru for what's been lent. The bell holds the time.
Meraa, mine. The fifth salok loosens the grip of this word: wealth, spouse and property, everything we call meraa, is not our companion all the way; know this as true.
Your line: none of it goes. Today, when you catch yourself saying my, my car, my desk, my time, add the word lent, and see how it changes your grip. Day five hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: The Sikh path is a householder's path of work, owning and sharing; the ninth Guru's salok on wealth, spouse and property is heard among his saloks at the bhog of a complete reading, including readings held after a death, as a reminder that nothing we own goes with us.

fork.setup: the salok names wealth, spouse and property. what does it say about them?
options: they are evil and should be given up.
none of them is your companion all the way.
they come with you if you earn them honestly.
fork.reveal: dhan daaraa sampat sagal, jin apunee kar maan: none of these is a companion. says Nanak, know this as true.

original.note: Gurmukhi: meraa, mine. The salok loosens the grip of this little word.

trapdoor: what you thought: none of it is yours means you shouldn't care about things or people.
what it means: it means everything, even the people we love, is lent, not owned, and none goes along at death.
what a scholar hears: the salok's daaraa, wife or spouse, is a Sanskrit-derived word common in Braj poetry, and Sikh commentators read the line as loosening possession, not love.
